clue.text: Conflict was backed by capital

parts.note: a conflict between nations is a war

indicators.note: something backed has been put into reverse, so the word before it is read from its end

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A war was supported by the people in the capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conflict was backed' reads as a war gaining support, but 'backed' acts only on the word just before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Warsaw is the capital city of Poland, so it is an example of a capital.

clue.text: Come away with several, being charming

parts.note: to come away with a prize is to win it
several and some both mean a few

explanation.surface: Someone leaves a party with several new friends, having been charming all evening.
explanation.definitionFit: Winsome describes an appealing, engaging manner, a close synonym of charming.

clue.text: Grins stupidly and made a telephone call

definitions.note: the clue's past tense does not match the answer, which is present tense

indicators.note: doing something stupidly means doing it in a muddled way, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone smiles foolishly while phoning a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is tense-shifted: RINGS means makes a telephone call, while the clue says made one.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring someone is the everyday British verb for phoning them up.

clue.text: Aim to take student to hospital department — because of this?

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one word goes into the other

parts.note: taken as written, opened up to hold a letter
L is the learner plate, so a student
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: Someone plans to take a student patient along to a hospital clinic, and asks why.
explanation.walkthrough: AI(L)M plus ENT. The question mark marks the definition as playful: an ailment is why you would go to the ENT department.
explanation.definitionFit: An ailment is an illness, the very reason someone ends up being taken to a hospital department.

clue.text: Plays guitar in the streets — it's odd!

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, so STS for streets
rum is old British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A busker playing guitar out on the streets strikes someone as strange.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum here is the British adjective meaning peculiar, not the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To strum is to sweep the fingers across guitar strings, so strums means plays guitar.

clue.text: Gift obtained, thanks to a fast time

parts.note: ta is informal British for thanks
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: Someone received a present, all because of a quick finishing time in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' suggests speed, but here it means going without food, as in Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift can mean a natural ability or flair, which is exactly what a talent is.

clue.text: A French mother, elderly, is not harmed

parts.note: un is French for a
a dam is the mother of an animal, such as a horse
aged means old, elderly

explanation.surface: An old French mother has come through unhurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Undamaged means suffering no injury or damage, the same as being unharmed.

clue.text: Strictly dressed, RN-style

indicators.note: dressed can mean prepared or arranged, as food or a shop window is dressed, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, hyphen dropped, seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Sailors dressed strictly in the manner of the Royal Navy.
explanation.walkthrough: RN is the Royal Navy, which makes the strict uniform picture convincing; the letters are only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Sternly and strictly are both adverbs describing a severe, uncompromising manner.

clue.text: Trouble at public lavatory?

parts.note: being at a place is being in it
a public convenience is the British euphemism for a public toilet

explanation.surface: Someone asks if there has been a problem at the public toilets.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks like a cryptic definition of a toilet mishap, but it splits neatly into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Inconvenience is bother or difficulty caused to someone, a direct synonym of trouble as a noun.

clue.text: Ann will accept a ring before long

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: taken as written, opened up to hold a letter
a ring is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: Ann is going to accept an engagement ring soon.
explanation.walkthrough: AN(O)N.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old-fashioned word meaning soon or shortly, the same as before long.

clue.text: Women you can put up with

definitions.text: Women you can put up with

parts.words: Women you can put up with
parts.note: surface reading: women whose company you can tolerate
setter's reading: put up means lodge, so these women give you lodgings

explanation.surface: A grudging remark about women who are just about tolerable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up with' looks like 'tolerate', but 'put up' also means stay as a lodger, so these are women you lodge with.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlady is a woman who lets rooms to lodgers, so you can be put up at her house.

clue.text: Medical Officer uses different hair stuff

parts.note: MO is the standard abbreviation for Medical Officer

indicators.note: making something different changes its form, so these letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, four letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The army doctor tries a new hair product.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousse is a foamy styling product combed through hair, so it is a kind of hair stuff.

clue.text: Mention mixture, the first true soothing preparation

indicators.note: a mixture is things stirred together, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the first means only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the opening letter of true

explanation.surface: Someone recommends a mixture, claiming it is the original genuine soothing remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixture' sounds like part of the medicine theme, but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An ointment is a greasy salve rubbed on skin to ease pain, a soothing medicinal preparation.

clue.text: Dick, the CID man

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dick is old slang for a private eye
second meaning: a plain-clothes officer in the police Criminal Investigation Department

explanation.surface: Introducing Dick, the man from the police investigation unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dick' reads as a man's name, but it is slang for a sleuth. The CID is the British police department staffed by plain-clothes investigators.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are names for an investigator who solves crimes: American slang and a British police officer.

clue.text: Former husband one has to scold and acquit

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
taken as written
to rate is an old verb meaning to scold angrily

explanation.surface: An ex-husband must tell someone off and then let them off.
explanation.walkthrough: RATE meaning scold is archaic (related to berate), a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To exonerate is to declare someone free of blame, which is what a court does in acquitting.

clue.text: Guy dancing is about 50, that's plain

indicators.note: being about something means surrounding it, so one piece goes around another
dancing letters move about and settle into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, three letters to rearrange
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A man dancing at fifty is a plain sight, the setter suggests.
explanation.walkthrough: Guy is also the setter's name, a sly self-portrait. UGY wraps around L.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain, said of a face, is a polite way of calling someone unattractive or ugly.

clue.text: Lover boy's painful back

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: sore means painful

explanation.surface: A romantic young man is complaining of a bad back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like the body part, but it signals reading SORE backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of love, usually pictured as a winged youth, hence a boy of love.

clue.text: Hug me when standing with a couple

indicators.note: in a down entry, standing upright means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written, then turned upward
a brace is a pair, as of game birds

explanation.surface: An invitation to embrace standing up, along with a couple of others.
explanation.definitionFit: To embrace someone is to wrap your arms around them, which is what a hug is.

clue.text: Insufficiently cooked, turned red inside: ruined!

indicators.note: inside means placed within another word

parts.note: undone means ruined or brought to disaster

indicators.note: turned means changed around, so the letters of the word before it are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, three letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A cook laments meat still red in the middle: the dish is spoilt.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all kitchen, but 'red' is letters to shuffle and 'ruined' supplies the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Underdone food has not been cooked for long enough, so it is insufficiently cooked.

clue.text: Bar with amber liquid to try!

indicators.note: something liquid flows and has no fixed shape, so the letters are free to rearrange

parts.note: taken as written, five letters to rearrange
to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: An invitation to a pub serving an amber drink to sample.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, which makes 'amber liquid' feel like beer; it is the definition, meaning a ban.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official ban, especially on trade, and to bar something is to prohibit it.

clue.text: Girl going in two directions to find goats

indicators.note: going in means entering, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: N and S are the compass points north and south
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl sets off in two directions looking for her goats.
explanation.walkthrough: N(ANNIE)S. 'Nannies' suggests childminders, but here they are female goats.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanny is a female goat, so nannies are goats, an example of the animal.

clue.text: Street water filter

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
rain is water falling from the sky

explanation.surface: A filter for the water that runs off the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water filter' reads as one device, but filter alone is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To strain a liquid is to pass it through a sieve, which is what filtering it means.

clue.text: Abraham sent note in; he's staying away

definitions.note: a clause standing for a noun: the person who is staying away

indicators.note: in means the words before it are placed inside another word

parts.note: Abe is the short form of Abraham
taken as written
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: Abraham sent a note to say he would not be coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abraham' tempts you to take the two-letter abbreviation straight off, but the whole short name is the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: An absentee is a person who is not present, so 'he's staying away' describes such a person.

clue.text: Bitter in big can

indicators.note: in means one word sits inside another

parts.note: taken as written, opened up to hold the can
a can is a tin

explanation.surface: A pint of bitter beer sold in a large can.
explanation.walkthrough: BI(TIN)G. Bitter is a British style of beer, which makes the drinks picture, but here it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A biting wind or remark is sharp and harsh, which is what bitter means used that way.

clue.text: A number — or the one who sings it?

parts.note: ten is a number
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is this a song, or the singer who performs it?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' has a second sense of a song, so the singer of it rounds off the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenor is a male singer with a high voice who performs a musical number.

clue.text: Furious Turkish commander's car gets here

parts.note: mad means very angry
an aga was an Ottoman Turkish commander, plus the possessive S
taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry Turkish general's car finally arrives at its destination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here' is the definition: the place the car gets to, in the reading of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Madagascar is the island nation the clue points to as the place where the car arrives.

clue.text: Artless devotee returns carrying one

indicators.note: returning means coming back the way it went, so the word is read backwards
carrying means holding something inside

parts.note: a fan is a devoted follower
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A simple-minded follower comes back holding something.
explanation.walkthrough: FAN reversed is NAF, which then holds I.
explanation.definitionFit: Naif, borrowed from French, means innocent and unsophisticated, which is what artless means.

clue.text: Looking at watch in front garden

parts.note: to eye something is to watch it
taken as written

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is used

parts.note: the opening letter of garden

explanation.surface: Someone examines a wristwatch they found in the front garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a timepiece and 'front garden' like a place; both serve the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeing something is studying it closely with your gaze, which is looking at it.

clue.text: Stage directors make these

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the theatre stage, as in treading the floorboards
second meaning: company directors together form a governing body

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests theatre directors building a set; 'stage' and 'directors' are in fact separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The boards is an idiom for the theatrical stage, and a company's directors sit on its governing board.
